## Does a Control Law Depend on How You Label the Coordinates?

Write a control law on a sphere in spherical coordinates, then transform to Cartesian—do you get the same closed-loop behavior? Of course you should. Yet naive implementations break. A metric—a rule for measuring distance—is the tool that makes control laws *coordinate-free*: they say the same thing no matter how you write the state. This is not pedantry; it is essential for systems like robots where natural coordinates (joint angles, end-effector positions) are related by nonlinear transformations.

## Introduction and Qualitative Purpose

This chapter reformulates tangent-space control and contraction statements on manifolds to avoid chart-dependent confusion.

## In Laymans Terms

We should describe control laws in a way that does not depend on arbitrary coordinate choices.

## Geometric Intuition

A Riemannian metric gives each tangent space its own inner product, and pullbacks transport task priorities into system coordinates.

## Pullback Construction

$$
M(x)=J(x)^\top W(h(x))J(x).
$$

If $J$ is rank-deficient, this is semidefinite; practical synthesis uses regularization or nullspace completion for strict positive definiteness.
